1.pericope_label: My son, keep my words: bind them upon thy fingers: say unto wisdom, Thou art my sister

schools.summary: Henry notices that this opening repeats an earlier one and ends at the same point, presses the finger-binding into a diamond ring, a signet and a wedding ring worn as the badge of espousal to God, argues from the tenderness of the eye against those who reproach strict walking as needless preciseness, since the law in the heart is the eye of the soul, and makes the strange woman sin itself, whose fallacies the word of God discovers.

Gill offers three figures for the binding on the fingers, the fingers’ ends, a thread tied as a reminder, and rings both memorial and ornamental, and a fourth sense that the fingers being instruments of action the command is to practise what is taught; he reads the strange woman literally and then of the idolatry and will worship of Rome, and takes the sister of the fourth verse for the Gospel and for Christ.

Clarke sets out the chapter in three movements, an exhortation to wisdom, the character of a harlot and her conduct toward a youth, and solemn warnings, explains the apple of the eye anatomically as the pupil so necessary to sight and so easily injured, and names the strange woman flatly as the prostitute and adulteress; Wesley reduces the finger-binding to a ring continually in a man’s eye.

Ellicott supplies the ritual behind the finger-binding, the phylactery thong wound seven times round the left arm and as many round the middle finger; Keil and Delitzsch report an extra couplet in the Greek after the first verse which disturbs the connection, discuss at length an accentuation of the imperative for which they say no reason is to be perceived, note that Hebrew and Arabic alike call the pupil the little man of the eye, and derive the window from a boring through of the wall and the lattice from a root meaning cool and fresh.

debates: What is the binding upon the fingers? Ellicott takes it against the background of the phylactery, whose thong was wound seven times round the arm and as many times round the middle finger; Gill offers a thread tied as a memorandum, rings that are memorial and ornamental, and the fingers as instruments of action so that the command is to practise; Henry makes it a diamond ring, a signet and a wedding ring, the badge of espousal to God; Wesley reduces it to a ring kept in view.

Who is the strange woman? Clarke names her flatly the prostitute and the adulteress; Gill takes her so and then allegorically of the errors, idolatry and will worship of Rome; Henry generalises her into sin itself, that flattering but destroying thing; Keil and Delitzsch keep her concrete and treat the following narrative as the author’s own observation.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch report that the Greek carries an extra couplet after the first verse, which they say disturbs the connection here.

Keil and Delitzsch record an accentuation of the imperative in the second verse that differs from its pointing elsewhere, resting on a Jewish grammarian and on certain manuscripts and printed editions, and say plainly that no reason for it is to be perceived.

Keil and Delitzsch note that Hebrew and Arabic alike name the pupil the little man of the eye, and derive the lattice from a root meaning cool and fresh, the shutter being what keeps off the rays of the sun.

Henry turns the tenderness of the eye into an argument against those who reproach strict and circumspect walking as needless preciseness, on the ground that the law in the heart is the eye of the soul.
themes: a command worn as a wedding ring
the pupil called the little man of the eye
an accent no one can account for
a woman read as a person and as a church
a lattice named for the coolness it keeps

6.pericope_label: For at the window of my house I looked through my casement, and beheld among the simple ones a young man void of understanding

schools.summary: Henry doubts the story is a parable and explains the window by the teacher’s magistracy, adds an aside on the profane poets of his own age who would make the harlot a heroine and the comedy end pleasantly, counts six faults in the young man from his youth to his hours, and draws the woman as loud, stubborn and impatient of any yoke, closing with the line that virtue is a penance to those to whom home is a prison.

Gill turns the three words for nightfall into a timetable of the young man’s journey, from twilight at his setting out to black night at the door, and reads the whole scene allegorically as well, the simple ones being the followers of antichrist, the corner being the chapels and synagogues to be avoided, and the woman being the mother of harlots who pretends to be the spouse of Christ.

Clarke renders the young man’s folly literally as being destitute of a heart, doubts that the woman was married at all and suspects her claim was a falsehood calculated to make him secure, and notes that sitting in an open place with the face covered was once the mark of a harlot; Wesley has the young man idle and careless near the corner where her house stood.

Ellicott judges the young man not yet vicious but only empty-headed, notes that the verb of his walking is used of the slow step of a religious procession, glosses the woman’s subtlety as feigning love to her husband and devotion to her lovers, and draws the moral that trifling from twilight till dark night leaves no excuse of sudden temptation; Keil and Delitzsch treat the narrative as the author’s own observation, insist the woman is a licentious wife and not a common street-walker, and defend the first word for nightfall against a critic by a rabbinic distinction between the evening and the morning twilight.

debates: Was the woman a married wife or a common prostitute? Gill, Henry and Keil and Delitzsch all take her for a wife, Henry adding that she lived in reputation among her neighbours and Keil and Delitzsch insisting she is no street-walker but a married woman who behaves as one when abroad; Clarke doubts it, holding that her claim to a husband and a house may have been a falsehood calculated to keep the young man from thinking he risked anything with a common woman, which he is rather inclined to believe, since she was subtle of heart.

Is the narrative fact or parable? Henry reports that it is supposed to be a parable or imagined case and doubts it was too true, and explains the window by the teacher’s office as a magistrate who inspected the manners of his subjects; Keil and Delitzsch treat it throughout as the author’s own observation, watched from where he stood.
outliers: Henry breaks off to say that such a story would serve the profane poets of his own age to make a play of, with the harlot for heroine, her arts celebrated as triumphs of wit, the comedy concluding pleasantly, and every young man in the audience coveting to be so picked up.
Henry closes his portrait of the woman with the line that virtue is a penance to those to whom home is a prison.

Gill reads the whole episode a second time as an allegory of the Roman church, making the simple ones the followers of antichrist, the corner to be avoided the Popish chapels, and the woman the mother of harlots who professes to be the spouse of Christ.

Keil and Delitzsch defend the first of the three words for nightfall against a critic who denies it can mean twilight, citing the rabbinic distinction between the evening and the morning twilight and allowing the root to cover the whole cool half of the day.
themes: a story told as evidence rather than invention
six faults counted in one young man
a marriage claimed and doubted
three words for one nightfall
a seduction read as a church

14.pericope_label: I have peace offerings with me: come, let us take our fill of love: for the goodman is not at home

schools.summary: Gill explains the peace offering as eucharistic, most of the victim returning to the offerer to be eaten the same day, so that the invitation is to supper, notes that the word can mean a consecrated woman and calls her a religious harlot, compares a poet’s phrase for eyes drunk with love, and supposes she avoids the word husband lest it raise a difficulty in the young man’s way or remind herself of her obligation.

Clarke separates the couch to recline on at meals from the bed to sleep on and reports an old version rendering the coverings painted carpets of Egypt, breaks with the received identification of the second spice on the ground that aloes is no perfume and proposes sandal wood, reports from a book of eastern customs that the gods are worshipped in brothels with the offerings divided among the women, and at the invitation itself declares the original too gross to be literally translated while printing it in the English of his old manuscript Bible; Wesley takes her offering as an advertisement of her larder.

Ellicott stresses that the peace offering was voluntary and admitted the offerer to feast with God, parallels the abuse of it with the desecration of the love-feasts at Corinth and of church-feasts nearer home, would render the coverings coloured or striped, traces myrrh to Arabia and aloes and cinnamon to Africa and Ceylon, observes that she does not even call the man her husband, and infers from the full moon a fortnight off that it must now be new moon when the nights are dark; Keil and Delitzsch weigh two derivations of the name of the offering, fix the bed as a wooden frame, describe the myrrh resin oozing through the bark, and call the whole speech the rhetoric of sin.

debates: What is the offering she names? Gill makes it eucharistic and the feast that follows the point of the invitation; Ellicott insists it was purely voluntary and admitted the offerer to feast with God; Clarke takes its spiritual design to be the making of peace between God and man; Keil and Delitzsch weigh a derivation from holding friendly relationship against one from discharging perfectly and prefer to call it a thank-payment or due-offering.

Is the second spice aloes or something else? Keil and Delitzsch take it as the Semitic form of an old Indian word for a wood whose scent lies in the root; Clarke objects that aloes is no perfume and proposes sandal wood, which is much used in the East; Ellicott places aloes and cinnamon on the east coast of Africa and in Ceylon without disputing the name.

When does the husband return? Ellicott takes the term for the full moon, a fortnight off, and infers that the night of the story must be a new moon, when the nights are dark; Keil and Delitzsch render it the same way; Clarke reports the Latin for the full moon and an old version for the day of the assembly and settles on the approaching festival; Gill draws nothing from the term and reads only the money bag as evidence of a long absence.
outliers: Clarke reports from a book of eastern customs that in many parts of the East the gods are worshipped in brothels, with fragments of the offerings divided among the women who keep them, and takes it as light on this verse.
Ellicott parallels the abuse of a religious festival here with the desecration of the love-feasts at Corinth and with the history of church-feasts among his own people.

At the invitation Clarke declares that his rendering does not half express the original, that he forbears, and that the Hebrew is too gross to be literally translated, and prints the speech instead in the English of his old manuscript Bible.
Ellicott, Keil and Delitzsch and Gill all remark that she says the man rather than my husband, and each gives a different reason for the omission.
themes: an offering used as bait
a translator who declines to translate
one omitted word that gives her away
a fortnight measured by the moon
spices traced to three continents

21.pericope_label: With her much fair speech she caused him to yield: her house is the way to hell

schools.summary: Henry sets the two roads against each other, the path of virtue strait, narrow, solitary and uphill against the way of the adulteress, green, broad and crowded with company, and presses the point that the command is not merely to keep the feet from those ways but to keep the heart from inclining to them.

Gill gives three reasons for the dart striking the liver, that it is the fountain of blood, the seat of lust so that the man is struck where his lust began, and possibly a figure for disease; he turns her much fair speech into much doctrine and compares a woman who called herself a prophetess, observes that the epilogue addresses children in the Hebrew and a son in three versions, and notes that the last verse has ways in the plural and that the word for the world of the dead often means the grave.

Clarke reports that the two verses of images have been variously translated and prints a scholar’s corrected version in full, with an ox, a dog, a deer and a bird, while declining to pursue the alterations that produce it, notices that the words rendered wounded and strong men mean soldiers and heroes and that many who distinguished themselves in field and cabinet were destroyed by their mistresses, and closes the chapter with a line about the chambers of death where pleasure is at an end; Wesley adds that the ox goes securely, as if to good pasture.

Keil and Delitzsch declare the text here confused, since the arrow attaches to neither the ox nor the man in fetters, refuse the Greek expedient of turning the fool into a stag, and rearrange the members instead so that the bird and the snare begin a new comparison; they also find the verb of straying to be the word the law of jealousy uses of a wife’s trespass, and decide that the word opening the last-but-one verse means many rather than great. Ellicott notes that the received sense of the second clause is gained only by transposing the original, and offers the literal alternative, as if in fetters to the place where fools are corrected.

debates: Is the text of the two verses about the ox, the fool and the bird in order? Keil and Delitzsch say the confusion continues here, since an ox led to the slaughter is not shot and a madman in chains is not being killed, report that the Greek solved it by turning the fool into a stag, refuse that change, and rearrange the members so that the bird and the snare begin a fresh comparison; Clarke prints a scholar’s corrected version with a dog and a deer added, says slight alterations of the Hebrew produce these differences and declines to pursue them; Ellicott says the received sense is gained only by transposition and offers a literal alternative that ends in a prison.

Does the word opening the verse about the casualties mean many or great? Keil and Delitzsch allow that the accentuation seems to favour taking it with the noun that follows, and decide for many on the strength of passages where the two words stand together in that sense; Gill and Clarke bypass the question and read the two nouns themselves as soldiers and mighty men, so that the ruined are men of riches, wisdom and courage rather than the weak.
outliers: Gill gives three reasons at once for the dart striking the liver: it is the fountain of blood and so of life, it is the seat of lust so that the man is struck where his lust began, and the wound may stand for a disease infecting the blood.

Keil and Delitzsch find the verb of straying in the epilogue to be the word the law of jealousy uses for the trespass of a wife, and hold it specially appropriate where a faithless wife has just been drawn.
Clarke observes that many who distinguished themselves in the field and in the cabinet have been overcome and destroyed by their mistresses, and that history is full of such examples.
Gill notices that the word for her much fair speech can be rendered her much doctrine, and turns the seduction into false teaching by comparing a woman who called herself a prophetess.
themes: a text rearranged rather than emended
a wound placed where the desire began
two roads described by their traffic
casualties counted as soldiers and heroes
a house named for where it goes
